summary: Describes the IANA considerations for RADIUS, that is, how values in its registries are assigned. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Numbers used in a login protocol need a keeper so no two things use the same one. This memo says how new numbers are handed out.

questions: how to get a new radius code
subtitle: How to assign new numbers in RADIUS authentication and accounting.

tldr.problem: RADIUS uses many numbered codes and attributes, and these need to be assigned carefully to avoid conflicts and ensure interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: This document specifies how the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) should register new Packet Type Codes, Attribute Types, and Attribute Values in the RADIUS namespace, using policies ranging from expert review to standards action.
tldr.outcome: Implementers now have clear guidance on which number ranges require what kind of approval, helping to manage RADIUS extensions in an orderly way.

today: RFC 3575 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2003 and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 2865 and has been updated in turn by RFC 6929. It remains the primary source for RADIUS IANA considerations.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.content:
RFC 3575 provides guidance to the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) on how to manage registries for the Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS), which is defined in RFC 2865. RADIUS is widely used for authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA) in networks.

The document reserves and allocates Packet Type Codes and specifies policies for registering new values in three RADIUS name spaces: Packet Type Codes, Attribute Types, and Attribute Values. The motivation is to prevent conflicts, ensure interoperability, and allow for future extensions without breaking existing implementations.
sections.eli5: RADIUS is a system for checking who you are on a network. Since many companies want to add their own new features, someone needs to keep track of which numbers are used. This RFC tells IANA (the number keeper) how to do that job.

sections.title: Terminology and Registration Policies
sections.content:
The document uses standard terminology from BCP 26: name space, assigned value, and registration. It defines several registration policies that IANA can apply.

For RADIUS, there are policies including Private Use (for internal or vendor use), First Come First Served (no review needed), Expert Review (a designated expert checks proposals), Specification Required (must have a written spec), IESG Approval (the engineering steering group approves), IETF Consensus (broad agreement needed), and Standards Action (must be in a published RFC). Different policies apply to different types of values.
sections.eli5: When someone wants a new number, IANA can either just give it to them, ask an expert to check it, or require it to be in a official document. The stricter the policy, the more careful the choice.

sections.title: Packet Type Code Allocation
sections.content:
Packet Type Codes range from 1 to 253. The original RADIUS specification (RFC 2865) allocated codes 1-5 and 11-13. RFC 3575 allocates codes 40-45 (for dynamic authorization extensions) and reserves codes 250-253 for experimental use, with 254-255 reserved for future use.

Several codes (6-10, 12-13, 21-34, 50-51) are reserved even though they have no IETF specification, to avoid conflicts with non-standard implementations already in use on the Internet. New Packet Type Codes require IESG Approval, the highest level of scrutiny, since a new packet type has significant impact on interoperability. The ranges 52-249 should be allocated first; later allocations can use 14-20, 35-39, and 46-49 if needed.
sections.eli5: RADIUS messages start with a type code (a number from 1 to 253) that says what kind of message it is. Some numbers are already taken, some are saved in case old software uses them, and some can be given out carefully when new message types are needed.

sections.title: Attribute Type and Attribute Value Allocation
sections.content:
Attribute Types have a range from 1 to 255, which is much smaller than Packet Type Codes. Most numbers from 1 to 100 are already allocated. Numbers 17 and 21 are marked as available for re-use, though it is recommended to use them only after all others are exhausted. The range 101-191 can be allocated by IETF Consensus, which requires broad agreement.

RADIUS also defines Vendor-Specific extensions (Attribute 26) so vendors can add their own attributes without claiming global numbers. Attribute Type values 192-223 are for experimental use, 224-240 for implementation-specific use, and 241-255 require Standards Action.

Attribute Values (meanings for specific attributes) can be much more numerous: each attribute can have up to 4 billion values (2^32). The Designated Expert can allocate new attribute values. However, the Service-Type attribute (attribute 6) is special: its values define new modes of operation, and allocations require IETF Consensus.
sections.eli5: Each RADIUS message carries attributes (extra information) tagged with a number from 1 to 255. These numbers are scarce, so most are already claimed. Vendors can also add their own attributes using a special vendor code, so they don't need to ask for new global numbers.

sections.title: Expert Review Process
sections.content:
When a Designated Expert must be consulted (such as for allocating new attribute values), the responsible IESG area director appoints the expert. The expert posts the request to the AAA Working Group mailing list (or a successor) for comment and review, including an Internet-Draft. The expert has 30 days to approve or deny the request, publish the decision to the mailing list, and inform IANA.

If a request is denied, the expert must explain the reasons and, when possible, suggest how to modify the proposal. The intention is that allocations will be accompanied by a published RFC, though the expert can approve allocations once it is clear an RFC will be published, allowing values to be allocated before the RFC is officially approved.
sections.eli5: An expert listens to proposals for new numbers, talks it over with other engineers for a month, then decides whether to allow it. If they say no, they explain why and suggest how to fix it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations detailed in BCP 26 apply to this document. Security considerations relating to RADIUS itself are discussed in RFC 2865, RFC 3162 (RADIUS and IPv6), and RFC 3576 (Dynamic Authorization Extensions).

The careful allocation of codes and attributes helps prevent interoperability problems that could arise if conflicting implementations use the same numbers, which could lead to subtle authentication or accounting failures.
sections.eli5: Giving out numbers in an orderly way prevents confusion and helps RADIUS work safely on networks.
